title: The Secret of Xylos
markdown:
The colony on Xylos sat under skies of twilight violet and rose. Its people told of a daring exodus from a crowded Earth, a bold leap to find a new home. For a long time that was the story everyone told.

Sable, an apprentice historian with a head full of questions and dust motes, spent her days in the echoing halls of the Grand Archives. She loved the faint scent of aged data-slates and the quiet hum of ancient machines. The sheer volume of knowledge, stacked toward the domed ceiling, both thrilled and daunted her.

One cycle, while cataloging a forgotten scanner nobody had bothered with for decades, her fingers brushed a hidden panel. A faint tremor ran up her arm. Breath caught. Something hidden. With a dusty click the panel sprang open, revealing a small warped data core. Its encryption was a tangled knot unlike anything she had encountered.

“Corrupted,” Archivist Thorne declared, a dismissive wave, face a mask of weary bureaucracy. “Best left undisturbed, Sable. We have official histories for a reason. They are curated for clarity.”

Sable did not much care for official when there was a whisper of hidden. She felt a certainty settle in her bones that this core held more than errors. Something important. Perhaps deliberately obscured.

The Archives’ tech was as old as the stories it housed, and just as temperamental. She needed someone who understood circuits. Someone who could coax life from dead metal. She needed Kit.

Kit’s workshop was not in the polished halls. It was a delightful mess of wires, spare parts, and half-finished contraptions, tucked in the bustling lower sectors. The air hummed with possibility. Ozone, oil, the metallic tang of ambition. Kit was all sharp angles and quick movements, hands stained with grease, eyes bright with an engineer’s unflappable logic. She saw problems as puzzles.

Sable, feeling like a misplaced artifact amidst the organized chaos, held out the warped object.

“I have a data core. Encrypted. They say it’s corrupted. I think it’s important.”

Kit turned it in nimble fingers, brow furrowed. She tapped it, listening to its silent response.

“Corrupted means interesting. What’s on it?”

“That’s the problem. I don’t know. I found it in a secret compartment, in an old scanner unused for years.”

Kit’s lips twitched into a rare almost-smile. “Secret compartments always mean a good story. Or trouble. Usually both.” She sighed, ruffling a pile of tools. A tiny wrench clattered. “All right, historian. What do you want me to do with this junk?”

“There’s an old memory drone. Forgotten annex, Sector Gamma. Its power core is failing, but its data banks are supposed to be intact. If we transfer this core to the drone, maybe it will tell us what it knows.”

They set off together. The drone, when they found it, was a sad utilitarian box of tarnished metal, dented and scarred, one dim flickering optical sensor that seemed to weep faint blue light. Kit set to work at once. Tools dancing. She rewired the failing power relay, purged residual data, and with utmost care integrated the mysterious core. A dance between old and new.

“This old thing is called Echo,” Kit announced, stepping back as it whirred to life. A low resonant hum filled the dusty space, vibrating in their bones. Echo’s single eye flickered, then glowed with a steady soft blue, as if awakening from a long slumber.

The memories began.

Not the crisp curated simulations Sable was used to. Fragmented, like shards of broken glass. A fleeting glimpse of a sky too orange and hazy to be Xylos. A cacophony of shouts, alarms, the roar of engines. Blurry faces etched with a fear she had never seen in sanitized texts.

“The Great Departure,” Echo rasped, a strange chorus of many lost voices. “They said it was for a new home. A promise of tomorrow.”

The fragments did not feel like a brave beginning. They felt like a desperate escape. Sable shivered, not of cold but of gnawing unease. The official story of hopeful pioneers began to feel thin.

“Why would they leave so many behind?” Kit murmured, watching a crowded spaceport, ships departing against a smog-choked sky. “If it was just a new home, why the panic?”

Over the next few cycles they worked tirelessly. Kit kept Echo powered, coaxing fragments, sometimes sitting up through the colony’s dim hours with a cable clenched in her teeth. Sable brought stolen printouts from the official ledgers and laid them on the floor like a second map. Departure dates that did not match. Passenger lists with names struck through and never restored. Coded references. Whispers of the Silence. Unforeseen contagion. The official histories mentioned overpopulation and resource depletion. These fragments spoke of something more immediate. A race against time. Once Echo showed a child’s toy left on a departure ramp. Kit turned the volume down and did not joke for the rest of that cycle.

Finally Echo played it. Not a fragment. A full unbroken recording. The drone’s eye focused with almost mournful intensity. The voice of Elara Vance, first leader of Xylos, the revered founder, filled the workshop. Her face, etched with unimaginable weariness, filled the viewscreen. Suffocating silence. Sable felt a lump in her throat. Ozone from the drone mingled with dry dust, a stark contrast to the raw grief in Vance’s voice.

“My dearest logs. If anyone ever finds this. If these fragmented echoes ever find their way out of the silence. I must confess. The truth is a far heavier burden than the lie. And the lie was for you.” She paused, swallowing, gaze seeming to pierce the years. “Earth is not merely struggling. It is dying. A contagion, swift and incurable, has swept the continents. There is no refuge, no cure, no hope left for those who remain. We had a chance. A singular agonizing chance to escape, to carry a fragment of humanity to the stars. But the choice…” Her voice broke. “The choice was to flee, knowing we could save only ourselves. We left millions behind. Not because we didn’t try. We tried. The odds were zero. The contagion was too virulent, too fast. We had to believe that some would find a way to endure. That our descendants would one day look back and not be consumed by the despair of our decision. We had to forge a future built on hope, not on the ashes of our failure.” A quiet lament. “I censored the true nature of our departure. To spare our children the crushing weight of this guilt. To give them a foundation of hope, not of abandonment. It is my deepest shame, my greatest sorrow, and my last desperate act of love for the future.”

Kit, usually so stoic, looked stunned. Tools forgotten. Sable could barely breathe. Sorrow for Earth’s fate. A dawning understanding of the terrible sacrifice. They had not just left. They had been forced to leave.

“They chose hope for us,” Kit whispered, voice rough. “Even if it meant carrying that secret all their lives.”

Sable looked at Echo, blue eye still glowing, a silent witness. “History isn’t just dates and events. It’s about the impossible choices people make.”

They knew they could not keep this secret. Not to condemn. To understand. To honor. To acknowledge the true genesis of their home.

That evening the twin moons of Xylos cast long silvery shadows. Sable packed the core in a cloth that had once wrapped a data-slate, as if softness could keep a confession from rattling. Kit wiped grease from her fingers and did not quite succeed. They climbed the ridge without talking much. Echo hovered nearby, a gentle hum, sometimes drifting ahead as if it already knew the view. Cool crisp air, the faint sweet scent of night-blooming flora. Below, a tram bell marked the hour the Archives closed. The colony a cluster of warm lights against deepening twilight.

“It’s bittersweet,” Kit said, gaze on the distant lights.

Sable nodded. A single tear caught the moonlight. “Yes. But it’s also real.” She looked up at the star-dusted canvas. They did not announce that love endured the darkest despair. They only stood until the moons had moved a finger’s width, Echo’s blue eye the steadiest light on the ridge, and tomorrow they would take the recording to the Archives, whether Thorne wanted curated clarity or not.
